p: Ana means to file in March, and the motion will land with Meredith Sloane, the chief deputy district attorney.
Ronnie Galvan, the bartender, still says her father swung first. He'd also swear her father walked out the back with nothing on his head, half an hour before the man in the cap.
At the bathroom sink Dani remembered something she'd never told anybody: the Sunday after, her father shaving at noon, with a scrap of tissue on his neck.
On the phone her father took her knight with his bishop, and told her again he drove straight home that night.
Teo pointed out that the man ran off on foot, and their father never walked anywhere he could drive.
Consuelo Baca. The neighbor across from the back lot, the State's eyewitness. She's eighty three now.
Alma Baca. Consuelo's granddaughter, a third grade teacher. She was eight that night, home sick with an earache.
Ana Brennan. Still working the case with Dani on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
Luis Ruiz. His bishop still sits on her knight's square, and neither of them brings it up.

Saturday, February 13. Consuelo Baca had called Ana's office three times on Tuesday and left three messages on the machine. Ana played them for Dani in order, standing by the desk with her arms folded, as if they were exhibits.

This is Consuelo Baca. I'll talk to the girl. Saturday, after the four o'clock Mass. A click. Then: Consuelo Baca again. Not after. Before. Two o'clock. My granddaughter says before. Then the third one, after a cough: Tell her come hungry.

I wrote her in January, Ana said. Letterhead. My name, my bar number, the works. She called back and asked for the girl. So you go alone, and you do the hardest thing there is to do with a witness. Which is? Nothing. Ask her what she saw. Then shut up. Write down her words, not yours.

Seventeen weeks to June. On Wednesday, February 3, Dani had made her move at last, and it wasn't the pawn. She'd brought a rook across instead, the long way, and on the other end of the line her father went so quiet she thought the call had dropped. Huh, he'd said. Last Wednesday he moved and she moved, and neither of them said a word about the bishop.

Thursday she'd told Teo on the phone where she'd be on Saturday. Across from the old lot. He'd said okay. Then he'd asked whether the floor down there was still wet, and she'd said it was fine, and he'd said it wasn't.
Dicta was asleep on the rug with her legs straight out, running somewhere. Ana stepped over her to get to the filing cabinet.
February on Federal. The dryers downstairs have been going since six, and the floor's warm enough that Dicta has given up the rug for the bare boards by the radiator. Pencil.

For four weeks I've handed you arguments. Somebody concluded something, and you found the conclusion and went after the step that got there. Tonight there's no step to go after. A lot of these questions give you a short passage with no conclusion in it at all. Just facts. A schedule, a rule, a few things somebody counted. The question asks what those facts let you say.
So you're the one drawing the conclusion now. Which means you're the one who can overreach.

There are two strengths of this question, and the stem tells you which. Must be true means the facts prove it. Not suggest it, prove it: if every statement in the passage is true, the answer can't be false. Most strongly supported is a notch softer. The answer doesn't have to be guaranteed. It has to be the one the facts back best, usually by a short step, and the other four will be either unsupported or too big.

Most of the time the right answer joins two facts. Every pilot at the flight school holds a medical certificate. Everyone who holds one has to see the doctor once a year. Tomás flies for the school. Nobody wrote down that Tomás sees the doctor every year, but it's sitting right there, and that's the answer. Look for a fact that hooks onto another one.

How the exam asks it. Must be true stems say that if the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true. Supported stems ask which choice the statements most strongly support, or which is most strongly supported by the information. Neither stem asks you to find a flaw or fix anything. Take the facts as given and draw from them.

The traps here are the opposite of the traps in a flaw question. There, you were told the argument was bad and the wrong answers defended it. Here, the facts are fine and the wrong answers say more than the facts do.

Watch the size of the words. All, always, never, only, the reason, proves. If the facts say most, the answer can't say all. If the facts say one thing happened after another, the answer can't say because. A choice can be likely, even true in the real world, and still go one step past the page. That one is wrong.

Watch the arrows. If every pilot at the school holds a certificate, that doesn't mean everyone with a certificate flies for the school. You know this from the flaw chapter. Here the reversed rule shows up as an answer choice that sounds exactly like a fact you were given.

And watch the counting words. Most and most can do something nobody expects. If more than half of a choir sings at the early service and more than half of the same choir sings at the late one, then at least one singer does both, because two groups that each take more than half of the same room have to overlap. Some plus some gives you nothing. Most plus most of the same group gives you some.

Could be true is its own trap. A choice that nothing in the passage rules out is still not a choice the passage proves. On a must be true question, could be true is wrong. It's only right when the stem asks for something that could be true.
How the exam asks it. Expect a choice that would be true if one more fact were added. Ask what you had to bring with you to make it work. If the answer is anything at all, cross it off.
The rarest of these asks the question upside down. Which one of the following cannot be true? Or, which could be true, except? Both are asking for the one choice the facts rule out.

Test each choice against the facts and ask one thing: does it contradict them? Not, is it unlikely. Unlikely things happen every day. A choice that's merely improbable could be true, so it isn't your answer. You want the one that can't stand next to the facts without one of them falling down.

Rules make this easy, if you know what a rule lets you do. If A, then B. You get one move for free: no B, so no A. If every dog in the kennel has had its shots, then a dog without its shots isn't in the kennel. Say a choice puts an unvaccinated dog in the kennel. That one can't be true.
Two accounts can work the same way. Put two people's stories side by side and ask what they can't both allow. Sometimes the answer is the thing everybody's fighting about.

How the exam asks it. These stems may ask which choice cannot be true, which must be false, or which could be true except one. Rewrite the except form in your head as cannot be true before you read the choices.

Rules link. If a man was at that curb at a quarter past eleven, he was near the lot. If he was near the lot then, he hadn't gone home before eleven. If he hadn't gone home before eleven, your father's story is wrong. Join the links, the end of one to the start of the next, and you get one long rule: at the curb means the story's wrong. The long rule has a contrapositive like any short one. If the story's right, he wasn't at the curb. That's the whole fight in one line, and the State never had to write it down.

The test hides its arrows in words. If, every, all and any point from the first idea to the second. Only if points at whatever comes after it: you sit at counsel table only if you're on the case means at the table, so on the case. Unless means if not: no testing unless the judge orders it means no order, no testing. No A is a B runs both directions. No juror is a witness, so no witness is a juror.

Two moves feel like logic and aren't. Turning the arrow around: every man on the crew wore the red jacket, but a man in a red jacket isn't therefore on the crew. Half of Denver was in red that night. And denying both sides: not on the crew doesn't mean not in red. The wrong answers on these questions are mostly those two moves, dressed up to sound like the rule you were given.

Then the counting words. Some means at least one. Could be one, could be all. It never means not all. Most means more than half, and that's it. Some plus some gets you nothing. Most plus most of the same group gets you some. Most of the bar in red, most of the bar from Boston: somebody in red was from Boston, because two halves of one room can't miss each other. Now the trap. Most of the bar was in red, and most of the red was Boston. You'd think that makes most of the bar Boston. It doesn't. That second most only counts the people in red, and that's a smaller room. So every time two counting words meet, I want you to ask, out of how many?

Now the harder translations, one step at a time. Step one is and and or with a not in front. Not both means at least one fails. He wasn't both at the bar and at home at ten: fine, he was in one place at most, maybe neither. Neither means both fail. He was neither at the bar nor at home: he was somewhere else. People swap those two all the time. Say them out loud until they're dull. Not both, at least one is false. Neither, both are false.

Step two is a rule with two parts on one side. If a man was on the crew and wore red, he was in the lot. Flip it and negate it, and the and turns to or. If he wasn't in the lot, then he wasn't on the crew or he didn't wear red. One of them failed. You don't get to say which, and that's where the points go. It works the other way too. If he was at the curb or at the bar, somebody saw him. Nobody saw him, so he wasn't at the curb and he wasn't at the bar. Both. An or on the front of a rule becomes an and when you flip it.

Step three is the hard words. Unless: cross it out, write if not, and that's the front of the arrow. The motion fails unless the lab finds a second profile means no second profile, the motion fails. Not the other way round. The only: the only people who may touch the exhibit are counsel means may touch it, so counsel. It doesn't say all counsel may touch it. The common error on all of these is running the arrow both ways because the sentence sounds fair. Here's one for your card. Everyone who testified was sworn, and nobody who was sworn lied. Join them, then flip the chain. If you wrote that anyone who lied didn't testify, you've got it.

How the exam asks it. Chains turn up in must be true, sufficient assumption and parallel questions. Rewrite each rule as an arrow before you combine them, then check every choice for an arrow that's been turned around or denied.

Reading Comprehension asks the same questions in different clothes. A detail question asks what the passage says. An inference question asks what it suggests, or implies, or what can be inferred. The second is the supported question from Logical Reasoning, with a longer passage.

The right inference is almost never far from the text. Usually it's a line from the passage said in other words, plus one small step. If you have to argue for an answer, it's probably too far. If you can put your finger on the line it comes from and say the step in five words, it's probably right.

One kind of inference is about what isn't there. A transcript is a list of questions somebody chose to ask. Read the questions, and you can often say what nobody asked. That's an inference, and a strong one, because the page is the whole record. You're not guessing what the witness knew. You're reading what she was given a chance to say.

And keep the voices apart, same as last time. What a witness said, what the officer wrote down, and what somebody else concluded from both are three different things, and an answer choice will try to hand you one dressed as another.

How the exam asks it. Inference stems use words like suggests, implies, and can be inferred. Detail stems use according to the passage, or the passage states. Before you answer, find the line, and decide whether the question wants that line or one step past it.

You've got the arrows. Now I want them fast, because on the hard questions the arrow is buried under a not, an and, an or and an unless, and the clock doesn't care that you're still translating. So here's every piece, one at a time, and then we stack them.

Start with denying, because everything else leans on it. To deny a sentence, ask what the world looks like if it's false, and say the smallest thing that makes it false. All the tenants signed the lease. False means at least one didn't. Not that none of them did. That's far more than you need. Some tenant signed. False means no tenant did. Most of the tenants signed. False means half or fewer did. Always becomes not always. Never becomes at least once. Put three lines on a card and carry it a week. All goes to some not. Some goes to none. Most goes to half or fewer.

Then and and or. Deny an and, and you get an or. It's false that the clerk was early and polite means she wasn't early, or she wasn't polite, or both. Not late and rude. Those are opposites, and an opposite isn't a denial. A clerk who walks in right on time, perfectly polite, makes the sentence false, and she isn't late or rude. Deny an or, and you get an and. It's false that the van was at the shop or in the lot means it wasn't at the shop and it wasn't in the lot. The not walks inside and the joining word flips. People get this one backward more than any other, and the test knows it. When a not crosses an and, the and turns to or. When it crosses an or, the or turns to and.

Now deny a rule. If it rains, the game's canceled. When is that rule false? Not when it stays dry. The rule says nothing about dry days. It's false only if it rains and they play anyway. So the denial of if A then B is A without B: a case where the front happens and the back doesn't. That's what a counterexample is, and it's why one rainy game played sinks the whole rule. What people want to say is the opposite rule, if it rains they play. Too strong. You only need the one game.

Next, the words that build arrows. Some words put what follows them on the front of the arrow. If, when, whenever, every, all, any, each, anyone who. Others put what follows them on the back. Only if, only when, requires, needs, depends on, must have, is necessary for. If you sit for the test, you registered. You sit for the test only if you registered. Sitting requires registering. Three sentences, one arrow: sit, then registered.

Only by itself works the same way as only if: what follows it goes on the back of the arrow. Only members may vote means vote, then member. Now set it next to all members may vote, which means member, then may vote. Same words, arrows pointing opposite ways. The only works the other way around. The only people who may vote are members means the same arrow, vote, then member, but this time the words right after the only, people who may vote, are the front. So carry two rules. Only, alone, marks the back. The only marks the front.

Unless means if not, and the if not goes in front. You can't park here unless you have a permit. No permit, then you can't park. Flip it: parked here legally, then you had a permit. Without works the same: no entry without a ticket means no ticket, then no entry. Until often does too. The pool stays closed until the lifeguard comes means no lifeguard yet, then closed. One warning. In ordinary talk unless sounds like it runs both ways, as if a permit guarantees you a spot. On the test it doesn't. The permit gets you past this one rule. There could be another sign about street sweeping on Tuesdays.

No A unless B gets its own line, because the double negative slows everybody down and principle questions love it. No one may board unless they have a ticket. Turn the no one into a person may not. A person may not board unless they have a ticket. Unless is if not, so no ticket means no boarding. Flip it, and anyone who boarded had a ticket. Short form: no A unless B is A, then B. Learn it as one block and stop working it out every time.

Two parts on one side stack the same way denial does. If you're a member and you've paid, you vote. Flip it, and the and turns to or: didn't vote, so you're not a member or you haven't paid. If you're a member, you vote or you send a proxy. Flip that one: didn't vote and didn't send a proxy, so not a member. Two pieces joined by and on the back can be split into two rules. If member, then vote and pay dues means if member, vote, and if member, pay dues. An or on the back can't be split. You only know that one of them happened.

Here's one with every piece in it. No applicant who lacks a reference will be interviewed unless they've worked here before. Peel it slowly the first time. The no and the unless work together: an applicant who lacks a reference and hasn't worked here won't be interviewed. Two pieces in front, joined by and. Flip it, and the and turns to or: anyone who was interviewed had a reference, or had worked here before, or both. Now ask it things. Jo was interviewed and has never worked here. She had a reference. Sam has a reference. Nothing follows. The rule never says what happens to people who have one. That empty spot is where the wrong answer lives, sounding sure of itself.

Last, the rule that runs both ways. If and only if, or exactly when. Members vote if and only if they've paid means two arrows: paid, then vote, and vote, then paid. You'll rarely see it said in those words, and when you do, both arrows are yours. When you don't, you get one, however fair the second one sounds.

To make it fast, drill it the boring way. Every night for two weeks, take three rules from anything, a lease, a school handbook, the sign on the bus, and do four things to each one. Write the arrow. Write the flip. Say what the rule doesn't tell you. Deny it. Ten minutes a night. By the end you'll stop translating. You'll just see it.

How the exam asks it. Conditional words cluster in must be true, sufficient assumption, flaw and principle questions. On a hard one, write the arrow and its flip in the margin before you read the choices. Then each choice is a match test: the arrow, the flip, or one of the two moves that only look like them.

One reading inference, slowly. A passage about a river town says the ferry stopped running in 1931, the year the bridge opened, and that the ferryman's family opened a store on the far bank that same year. The question asks what can be inferred.

The choices, the way they'd come. The bridge put the ferry out of business. Likely, and too far. The passage gives you two events in one year and never says one caused the other. The ferryman's family had lived on the far bank before 1931. Not stated, and nothing points to it. In the years before 1931, someone crossing the river there could have used the ferry. That's one short step: the ferry ran until 1931, so in those years it was there to use. That's the inference. The store did better than the ferry had. Nothing compares them. The town grew after the bridge opened. Not in the passage at all.

Notice that the right answer is the dullest one. It's nearly a restatement, with one small step. The two that tempt you are the ones that tell a story, the bridge killing the ferry and the family moving. Stories are what the passage left out. When an inference choice makes you think and that's why, ask where the because is written. If it isn't, the choice is reaching.

How the exam asks it. Inference stems say the passage suggests, implies, or most strongly supports something. Find the line, take one small step, and drop any choice that needs a cause or a motive the passage never states.

Ana came back from the cabinet with the dispatch log in its plastic sleeve and laid it on the desk next to Gene's notebook, still zipped in its freezer bag. She put one finger on the second line and kept it there.

Dispatch log, Saturday, October 27, 2007, page two. Eleven seventeen and thirty eight seconds: 911 call received. The caller, C. Baca, lives across from the rear lot of the Night Owl Tap, on Highway 2. Eleven seventeen and fifty two seconds: the caller says a male, red jacket, ball cap, struck the victim with an unknown object, and the subject fled on foot. Eleven eighteen and twenty seconds: the victim is down at the curb, not moving. Medical requested. Eleven eighteen and forty one seconds: unit two fourteen en route.

Before you sit in that woman's kitchen, you know to the word what she already said. Otherwise she'll tell you something old and you'll think it's new. Or she'll tell you something new and you'll miss it. What does this line state? Not what it means. What it says.
A. That the man in the cap hit Travis with something heavy, like a pipe, and then ran off from the curb.
B. That the caller saw the man's face clearly enough but didn't know who he was by name at the time.
C. That the man in the cap ran north from the curb, toward the ditch and the railroad tracks behind it.
D. That the caller reported a man in a red jacket and a ball cap hitting someone and running off on foot.

A man in a red jacket and a ball cap hit somebody and ran off on foot, Dani reads. That's it. That's the whole line. Ana lifts her finger. Red jacket. Ball cap. Struck. On foot. Four things, at eleven seventeen, from a woman with a sick kid and a phone in her hand. Anything she tells you today, check it against those four.

That's the one. Pencil down. Specific detail. The line says the caller reported a male in a red jacket and ball cap who struck the victim with an unknown object and fled on foot. That's all four facts and nothing added. It records what she said, not that it happened.
Ana pulled Ronnie's statement from Phil's box and set it under the log, so the two times lined up. Eleven seventeen at the top. Eleven forty at the bottom.

Here's what I've got. Of every police paper we have, Ronnie's is the first one with your father's name on it. Twenty to twelve. The log is eleven seventeen. Take both times as right. She held up the pencil. Must be true. Not likely. Not probably. Must. What does that give you?
A. "She told Gene about the cap again on Sunday morning, at her house, when he came over to see her."
B. "The man who hit Travis really did have a ball cap on his head that night, whatever else he wore."
C. "She said cap at 11:17, twenty three minutes before Pa's name is on any police paper we have."
D. "Pa couldn't have been the man she saw. Pa never once wore a hat in his whole life."

So on paper, the cap comes first, Ana says. Before anybody wrote his name down, she'd already said cap. When she said cap there wasn't a name on any paper for it to help. That's not a probably. That's arithmetic. Why she said it is a different question. She writes 11:17 BEFORE 11:40 under CAP on the board, small.

Right. Now say why. Must be true. Join the two facts. The cap is in the log at eleven seventeen, and the name first appears at eleven forty. So on these papers the cap came first. Nothing is added and nothing is guessed.
Then Ana took a page out of Phil's trial binder and laid it beside the freezer bag. Gene's notebook on the left. The trial on the right.

Trial transcript, Monday, June 2, 2008, direct and cross examination of Consuelo Baca. Question: Mrs. Baca, where do you live? Answer: Across the street from the Night Owl. Behind it, across from the back lot. Question: Were you awake at about a quarter past eleven on the night of Saturday, October 27, 2007? Answer: Yes. My granddaughter had an earache. I was at the kitchen sink. Question: What did you see? Answer: A man hit another man by the curb, with something in his hand. The man fell down. The other one ran. Question: What was the man who ran wearing? Answer: A red jacket. Question: Did you see his face? Answer: No. I never saw his face. Question: What did you do? Answer: I called 911. Thank you, Mrs. Baca. Cross examination by Mr. Abrams. Question: Mrs. Baca, you can't tell this jury who that man was, can you? Answer: No, sir. Nothing further.
Seven questions, counting Phil's, Ana said. Read it against Gene's page. What did she tell somebody in 2007 that this page tells you nobody asked her in 2008?
A. She was asked about the cap on the stand and forgot to mention it in her answer.
B. She was never asked whether the man had anything on besides the red jacket.
C. She was never asked how she could make out the jacket's color from across the street.
D. She was never asked whether she'd seen the face of the man who hit Travis Hensley.

What was the man who ran wearing? A red jacket. And the next question is about his face. Nobody asked, anything else? She'd said cap to dispatch, and cap to Gene, and the State had stopped one word short of it. So had Phil.

Good. That's how you read it. Inference. One open clothing question, one answer, and no follow up. Nobody asked "anything else?", so the cap she gave dispatch and Gene never came up. The transcript never says so. Read the questions and it's there.
Decision four. Where the questions start.
Ana unzipped the freezer bag, the whole length of the seal, and turned the notebook to Consuelo's page, the one Gene started at five past nine. C. Baca, 64. And in the margin, in Gene's pencil, boy?

He wrote that on a Sunday morning, sitting with her, and in December he couldn't tell you why. She laid the pencil across the transcript at the second question, and Dani read it again under the lead. Were you awake at about a quarter past eleven on the night of Saturday, October 27, 2007? Now look where the questions start. Then tell me what that gives you.
A. Whatever she saw or heard before a quarter past eleven, nobody asked her about it.
B. Phil asked her about the earlier part of that night, and she couldn't remember any of it.
C. The State didn't want the jury to hear about anything earlier that night in the lot.
D. She told the jury she'd been standing at the sink since before the bar fight began.

A quarter past eleven, Ana says. First question after her address, and they put her at the sink at the moment they needed. Before that, the jury got nothing. If Gene's boy was anywhere, he was in the part nobody asked about.

That's the one. Pencil down. Inference. The prosecutor's first question about the night begins at a quarter past eleven, and nothing goes earlier, on direct or cross. So the transcript implies she was never asked about anything before then.
She was early. She was always early. At 1:35 she parked on the far side of Highway 2, facing the vape shop that used to be the Night Owl, and turned off the engine and didn't get out.

The back lot was paved now, and striped. Six cars. A dumpster with a padlock. Across the street from it, small and yellow, with a chain link fence and a plaster Virgin by the steps, was the only house on the block.
Twenty five minutes. She opened the practice set on her phone, because that was what she did with twenty five minutes.

Practice set, question 9. Night nurse's log: The patient in Room 4 rang the call bell at 2:10, 2:40, and 3:15 A.M. Each time, the nurse found the window blind rattling in the draft from the heating vent and found nothing else wrong. Maintenance taped the blind down at 3:30. The patient did not ring again before the shift ended at 7:00 A.M. The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
Her mother had worked nights her whole life. Her mother would have taped the blind herself at 2:10 and not written it down.
A. Taping the blind down is what let the patient sleep through the rest of the night.
B. The patient rang the bell only over the blind, and for no other reason.
C. The heating vent in Room 4 was set way too high that night and needs to be repaired.
D. Most likely, the rattling blind was at least part of why the patient rang.

Three rings, one rattle each time, nothing else wrong, and then the tape and no more rings. It doesn't prove the blind did it. It points there, and it points nowhere else. Most likely, at least part. The small words did the work.
Right. Now say why. Most strongly supported. The pattern backs a modest causal claim: the blind was likely involved. "Most likely" and "at least part" keep the claim inside what the log shows.

Alma Baca had the door open before Dani got to it. Twenty seven. Hair scraped back. Red pen behind one ear, uncapped. She looked at Dani the way she probably looked at a kid sent down to the office for somebody else's fight. She's eighty three. One hour. If she gets tired, you go. Okay. I mean it. I know you do.

The kitchen smelled like cumin and the comal. Consuelo Baca was small and straight in a cardigan buttoned to the neck, and she didn't let Dani say one word until there was a bowl of albóndigas in front of her and a tortilla on top of the bowl to keep it warm. Eat. Then. Alma sat at the end of the table with a stack of spelling tests and didn't grade one of them.
Dani ate. Then she asked what she'd come to ask, and only that. What did you see.

Consuelo told it looking at the window over the sink, not at Dani. The sink, the earache, the man by the curb, the thing in his hand. The detective asked me how tall. I told him I couldn't say. I couldn't. There was nothing out there to measure him by. She turned her hands over on the table. Only the other one. The other one was a big man. Big in the shoulders. And this one was smaller than him. That I saw. Smaller.
What does Dani say to Consuelo about how big the man in red was?
A. "Was he about my dad's height? Pa's about five ten, I think."
B. "So he was smaller than the man he hit. That's what you could see."
C. "So he wasn't tall enough to have been my father, then. Was he, Mrs. Baca?"
D. "So he was a small man, then. Short. Not a big man like the other one."

Yes. Consuelo nods once, hard, like a drawer shutting. Smaller than the big one. That's all. Write that. Dani writes SMALLER THAN THE BIG ONE. It fits her father. It fits half the men in Adams County. That's what it's worth, and she writes it at that size.

Good. That's how you read it. Most strongly supported. Her account backs one comparison, the attacker against the victim. It doesn't give a height and it doesn't rule anyone in or out. Dani keeps it exactly that size.
And before. Before the one in the jacket. Consuelo said it almost in passing. The little boy.

Ten minutes to eleven, by the stove. Alma's drops were at eleven, every four hours, and I was watching the clock for them. Out there in the lot. Papi. Papi. Like that. She said it softly, in a small voice, and it was worse than if she'd said it loud. Not screaming. Past screaming. You know how they get. I went to the glass. At night, with the light on in here, all you see is yourself and the stove. Out there, the trucks, dark. Then she was crying for me too, so I went to her.

I told the young policeman at the door. He wrote in his little book and he said, that's some kid from the apartments, ma'am. Some neighbor's kid. I said, what neighbor's kid is out at eleven o'clock in the back of a bar on a Saturday, crying for his papi? He said, yes ma'am. She shrugged. The detective wrote it too, the next day. Then nobody asked me again. Not ever.
Boy? In the margin. Nineteen years in a gun safe.
What does Consuelo's memory of the boy most strongly support?
A. "So a little boy was out there in the lot that night, crying for his papi."
B. "So some kid saw the fight inside the bar, and it scared him half to death."
C. "So it was a neighbor's kid, from the apartments, like the officer wrote it."
D. "So the boy saw the man in the jacket hit Travis. He was a witness too."
Yes. That. Dani writes it down. BOY. PAPI. 10:50. She underlines 10:50 twice, and she doesn't write anything else.

That's the one. Pencil down. Most strongly supported. What she heard backs a child in the lot, in distress, calling "Papi." That's the claim at the size of the evidence. It names no one, and it doesn't say why he was crying.
Ten to eleven. Teo was at Abuela's. Everybody knew where Teo was.
Consuelo got up and took Dani's bowl to the sink, and stood there with it, looking out. Come see.

It was a small window. A geranium in a coffee can, a dish rack, the plaster Virgin's twin on the sill, faded to the color of milk. Through the glass, the paved lot. The new curb. A row of parking stripes. At the curb stood a light pole, and on the pole, zip tied at about shoulder height, were two purple Rockies pennants, one faded nearly pink and one under it still dark.

His sister, Consuelo said, before Dani could ask. Every October. She never knocks. I leave the porch light on so she can see to do the ties. Dani had never thought of anybody standing at that curb on purpose. She'd seen his sister once, across a courthouse hall in 2008, with her purse in both hands. Dani had been the one who looked away.

The refinery men parked there in a row. Every Saturday. Trucks, trucks, trucks. And he ran that way. She pointed with the bowl. North. Past the end of the stripes there was a chain link fence with a gap in it, and past the fence a ditch, a long gray trough of ice and dead cattails, and past the ditch the rail bed, raised up on its gravel, and the tracks. Past the tracks, a long way off, the refinery. Its lights never go off. In the daytime you can hardly see them. Nothing in between. No street. No driveway. Nowhere a truck could go.

There's nothing back there. The ditch. The tracks. The kids go back there to drink. The young policeman and the other one walked it that night with their flashlights, all the way to the tracks. They didn't find anybody. Not a thing in his hand, not a thing on the ground.

In January, on the basement floor, Teo had said on foot, and men with trucks drive, and she'd wondered what was north of that lot. She didn't need a map now. She put it the way Ana would, only what had to be true: the man ran north on foot, and north there's nowhere to drive.
Taking that as true, which of these must also be true?
A. The man who ran away from the curb didn't have a truck anywhere that night.
B. The man ran back there to hide whatever he'd used, and then circled around.
C. If that was Pa, then he ran on foot to a place his truck had no way to get to.
D. The man who ran from the curb wasn't Pa, because Pa's truck was parked right there.

If. That's all she gets to keep, and it's enough. The State's man ran away from a row of trucks into a ditch, and the State's man drove a truck. Nobody in 2008 had to explain that. North was a word in a report. Nobody stood at this sink and looked. She writes NORTH, NO ROAD and dates it.

Right. Now say why. Must be true. Whoever ran north went where no truck could go. So if the man was Luis, he went where his truck couldn't follow. That's guaranteed by the facts, and it's conditional. It doesn't claim the man wasn't Luis.
Back at the table. The clock, Dani said. Just that. What time, and how she knew it.

That one. The stove: white enamel gone yellow at the knobs, a clock set in the back panel, its second hand still going round. Ten to eleven, the boy. I was watching it for the drops. Eleven, drops. Then I sat on her bed and sang her the whole song. Twice. Three times. Till she quit. She smiled down the table at Alma, who was reading one spelling test very hard. Then up to rinse the dropper. That's when. At the sink.
Did you hear the boy again? No. Not after. I listened. I sang and I listened.
What does the stove clock tell Dani about the crying?
A. "So by the time the man in the jacket came out to the curb, the boy was long gone."
B. "So he was crying because of the fight inside, at twenty five after ten."
C. "So whatever made him cry happened before eleven, before the man in red."
D. "So the boy was out there crying right when the man in the jacket hit Travis."

Yes, Consuelo says. Before. A long time before. Three songs' worth. Dani draws it like Ana would, a line and two ticks. 10:50, boy. 11:15, jacket. Two things on one night, and half an hour between them that nobody ever wrote down.
Good. That's how you read it. Most strongly supported. Boy at about 10:50. Attack after the eleven o'clock drops. So whatever set him off came first. That much the clock gives you. Not why.

Ten to three. Alma had looked at the stove clock twice, and the third time she said Abuela in the voice you'd use on a third grader stalling at the pencil sharpener. Consuelo waved her off. Dani was putting the cap back on her pen, and before she could close the notebook Consuelo leaned over and set a hand on it.

You were the girl, she said. At the courthouse. In the hall, in that blue dress. Somebody should have hemmed those sleeves. Dani said she remembered the dress. Her mother had bought it the night before, on sale, a size up so it would last. I read what you said in the paper, Consuelo said. The jacket and the washer.

All I said was red. I said it to the police and I said it to the jury, and then the man in the tie got up and said it ten more times, and every time he said it he got closer to your father's name. She looked straight at Dani for the first time since the door. They used my words too, mija.
A. "You should have told them you weren't sure the jacket was really red."
B. "You told them what you saw. They're the ones who said whose jacket it was."
C. "So you think they convicted the wrong man. You've thought so all this time."
D. "None of it was your fault, Mrs. Baca. You have to know that. Not any of it."

Yes, Consuelo says, and holds on to Dani's wrist for a second. That's right. I said red. I never said a name, not one time, and I'd swear to that in front of anybody. At the far end of the table Alma pushes her chair back, goes to the sink, and stands there running the tap with her back to them.

That's the one. Pencil down. Would agree with. She says it: "I said red," and the name came from someone else. Dani's reply puts the line where Consuelo puts it. What she saw, her side. Who it was, theirs.

At the door Consuelo put a hand on each side of Dani's face, the way you'd check a child for fever. Yours too, mija. They used yours too. Dani thanked her. She'd meant it when she said it to Consuelo. Coming back the other way, she couldn't take it.
Alma walked her out. On the porch she pulled the door shut behind them, almost all the way, and spoke low.

She went to confession every Saturday for a year after that trial. Every Saturday. She hadn't done anything. She looked across the street at the lot. Don't bring her into this for nothing. It isn't for nothing. Alma held her eyes a second longer than was comfortable. I remember the song, she said. Nothing else. I've tried. For her, I've tried. She went back in.

In the car Dani left the engine running for the heat and called Ana. She read her the notebook page, her own, word for word. Smaller. Papi. Ten to eleven. North, and nothing back there. When she got to Papi, Ana didn't say anything for long enough that Dani heard Dicta's tags rattle somewhere behind her.

Her words, Ana said finally. Write all of it out tonight. Hers. Not yours. Then, briskly: Now the record. What the jury had. Ronnie, out the back at a quarter to eleven. Consuelo, a man in red at the curb at a quarter past. The State, that man was your father. Take all three as true. What has to be?
A. "That Pa lied to Gene when he said he drove home alone at a quarter to eleven."
B. "That Pa was the only man in a red jacket anywhere near that lot that night."
C. "That Pa went back inside the bar sometime after Ronnie told him to leave."
D. "That Pa was near the lot, or back at it, half an hour after he left the bar."
Line four, Ana says. Near the lot at 11:15. Nobody ever proved it. They didn't have to. If all three are true it just is, and the jury filled in the half hour by itself.

Right. Now say why. Must be true. If he went out the back at 10:45 and he was the man at the curb at 11:15, then at 11:15 he was there, whether he stayed or returned. Nothing more is needed, and nothing more follows.

Now his, Ana said. Say your father's right. He was in the truck and gone before eleven, and he didn't come back that night. And say Consuelo's right about a quarter past. Put them side by side. Which of these can't be true?
Over at the house the front curtain moved. Alma, checking. It didn't close all the way.
A. "That Pa was the man who hit Travis at the curb and ran north on foot."
B. "That Pa threw a punch at Travis inside the bar at twenty five after ten."
C. "That the man who ran wore the same red jacket all the refinery men wore."
D. "That Pa had a ball cap on his head at some point that night, even for a minute."

That's the one, Ana says. And it's why nobody in 2008 ever put a minute on when he drove away. Pick any minute before 11:15 and they'd need him coming back. They never had to say it, so they never did.

Good. That's how you read it. Must be false. If he was gone before eleven and never came back, he wasn't at the curb at a quarter past. So he can't be the man Consuelo saw. Take both accounts as true, and it's the one claim that can't be.

Quarter to four, the door. Alma, and her grandmother in the good coat, for the four o'clock. Alma reached back in and hit the porch light, for later. Consuelo saw the car. One hand up, small, like at a bus stop. Dani put hers up too.
She didn't go home. Two miles, and she couldn't. Up Highway 2 to the refinery gate, turn around in the gravel, back down past the lot, up again. Radio off. Till the light went.

It was dark by the time she turned onto her own street, a little before six. The streetlight in front of the house had been flickering since Christmas, and in one of the flickers she saw it, and drove past her own driveway, and had to back up.

The washer was on the curb. The old one. Avocado green, the color of the whole house in 1990, sitting on a flattened box by the mailbox with its lid shut and its hoses coiled on top. A strip of duct tape across the front, in black marker, in capitals she'd know anywhere. LEAKS.

She went in through the side door and down the stairs without taking her coat off. The floor at the bottom was dry. It had been wet for a month and now it was dry, mopped, and there was a white washer where the green one had been, not new, a few years old, with a scuff on one corner and the hoses tightened down and the whole thing level. The shop vac was gone. On the lid, folded in a square, was one of his shop rags.
A text from Teo. that thing was leaking. dont make it a thing
She read it standing in the basement. In her head Consuelo was still saying smaller, smaller than the big one, the only measurement she'd ever been willing to give. She read Teo's text again.

She went back out to the curb. Cold enough now that the box under it had frozen to the grass. Her hand on the lid. Fifteen, a Sunday, eight in the morning: this lid, this drum, a red sleeve stuck to the side of it. And later, in a room full of strangers, because it was true. In the washer, downstairs. It was wet. The cycle was done.
She lifted it. Empty. No, one sock. Hers, gray, plastered to the drum since January probably. Into the coat pocket.
Inside: the bathroom towels, the dish towels off the oven door, his rag. All of it in together. The dial turned the wrong way, the opposite of the old one, which cost her a minute and one bad word.
It filled quiet. The old one used to bang like somebody was locked in it. Two steps up from the bottom, her Wednesday step. She watched the concrete.

Phone out, after a while. Thank you, she typed, and looked at it, and killed it. Ok. Sent. Then the notebook on her knee and Consuelo's words, all of them, Consuelo's and not hers, the way Ana wanted, while the water ran.
She stayed till the spin cycle. To be sure. Nothing came out from under it.
